name: Chemical reconstruction of skin scars
lead: Chemical reconstruction of skin scars (CROSS) is a focal technique in which a high-concentration trichloroacetic acid (TCA) solution is applied to the base of individual atrophic scars, such as ice-pick acne scars, rather than to the whole face.
Evidence in the sources reviewed is limited to small registered trials. Wikipedia lists TCA as a medium-depth peel agent used in office settings.[1]
infobox: Focal TCA application for atrophic scars

paras: Wikipedia describes TCA as a medium peel, often performed in an office or outpatient setting with more discomfort than light peels, and lists acne scars among peel indications.[1] The focal CROSS variant is not described on that page.

A completed registered trial (NCT07028567, 13 participants, started 2023) compares subcision followed by diluted calcium hydroxylapatite injection with subcision followed by a painted CROSS TCA technique for atrophic acne scars.[2] No results were available in the sources reviewed.
Peels generally can cause prolonged redness, pigment change, atrophy and scarring.[1]

refs.title: Subcision Followed by Diluted Calcium Hydroxylapatite Injection Versus Subcision Followed by Painting CROSS TCA Technique for the Treatment of Atrophic Acne Scars (NCT07028567)

card.summary: Spot-applying strong TCA acid into individual acne scars; studied in small trials.
card.note: Clinician procedure; sources found are thin.

quick.overview:
CROSS places a strong TCA solution into individual depressed scars, mainly acne scars, instead of peeling the whole face.

Only small trial registrations were found in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: The acid is said to trigger a focal wound-healing response in the scar base.
quick.risks: TCA peels can cause redness, pigment change and scarring. The technique is performed by clinicians.
